segments.text: The first Latin word — and it already contains save, safe, and salute.
Latin is read as written, every letter sounded. A macron (ā ē ī ō ū) marks a long vowel — held longer, same quality. Classical v = w. So salvē = SAL-weh, not "sal-vay."

Salvē (to one person) / salvēte (to several) is the imperative of salvēre, "to be in good health," from salvus "safe, sound, whole." To greet in Latin is to wish someone health. That root fans out into English — save, safe, salvage, salvation, salute, salubrious, the toast "salut!" — and into the Romance children as the word for health itself: Spanish salud, Italian salute, French salut.

salvē vs. salvēte: Latin changes the ending to mark one listener (-e) versus many (-ēte). This is the feature that defines Latin — meaning carried in endings, not in word order or extra words. English lost almost all of it; its Romance grandchildren kept some. You will meet it in every chapter.

segments.text: Point to salvē and say it once: SAL-weh. The model stays on the page.
Copy salvē once on the line below it. Write salve first, then add the short macron over the final ē. Look back at the model whenever you want.
Say the word as you finish. The macron belongs to the vowel: it records the long sound you already heard; it is not a new letter and not something to guess.
Compare your copy with the model. If one mark differs, repair only that mark. No hiding, no spelling from memory, and no second word today.
The ceremonious greeting — the one you still hear in Ave Maria.
Avē = AH-weh (again the w-sound for v). Two syllables, the second long.

Avē is the more formal greeting — "hail" — from avēre "to fare well, to be eager." It survives in English essentially unchanged inside the prayer "Ave Maria" ("Hail, Mary"), and stands in Catullus's famous avē atque valē — "hail and farewell" — spoken at his brother's grave, pairing the word you say on arrival with the one you say on leaving (next lesson).
Avē carried rank and ritual — addressed to emperors and gods (avē, Caesar). For an everyday "hi," Romans reached for salvē; avē was the bow, not the wave.

Latin's goodbye wishes you strength — and hides inside value, valid, and prevail.
Valē = WAH-leh. Like salvē, a health-and-strength wish frozen into a command.

Valē (singular) / valēte (plural) is the imperative of valēre, "to be strong, to be well." So goodbye in Latin literally wishes you strength. The root is an English gold mine: value, valid, valiant, valour, valence, prevail, convalesce, ambivalent ("strong both ways"). And the Romance children carry valēre as their verb "to be worth": Spanish valer, Italian valere, French valoir.

salvē, avē, valē are all the same shape — a bare imperative, a command form of a verb about health or strength. Latin doesn't say "hello/goodbye"; it orders you to thrive. Feel the -ē / -ēte pair recur: know it once, and you can address one friend or a whole room in any of the three.

lessons.title: grātiās (tibi) agō — "thank you" (I give thanks)
lessons.gloss: thank you (lit. "I give thanks to you")

segments.text: Say this and you have said grace, gratitude, gracias, and grazie all at once.
Grātiās = GRAH-tee-ās; agō = AH-go. In classical Latin c and t before i stay hard — GRA-tee, never "GRA-shee."

The full phrase is grātiās tibi agō — literally "I give thanks to you" (grātiās "thanks," tibi "to you," agō "I do/drive"). The noun grātia means "favour, grace, gratitude," from grātus "pleasing, thankful." Into English: grace, gratitude, gratis, grateful, gracious, ingratiate, congratulate. And straight into the Romance "thank you" you already learned — Italian grazie, Spanish gracias, Portuguese graças — all just the plural grātiās, "thanks," worn smooth.

agō means "I do" — the -ō ending is "I," so no separate pronoun is needed. This is Latin's great habit: the verb ending tells you who acts. Agō itself is a root you know: agent, act, agenda ("things to be done"), agile, navigate.

A surprise: Latin had no plain word for "yes." Here is what Romans said instead.
Ita = IH-tah; nōn = nōne, with a long ō.

Classical Latin had no simple "yes." To agree you said ita ("thus, so"), sīc ("so, in this way"), certē ("certainly"), or you just repeated the verb — asked "are you coming?", you answered "I'm coming." It was sīc that hardened into the Romance "yes": Spanish and Italian sí / sì, French si (the emphatic yes). "No" is easier: nōn ("not"), from older ne-oenum "not one thing" — the ancient negative ne- that also gives English no, not, none, never, and which you will meet again as Sanskrit na and Hindi nahīṇ.

A language that carries so much in its verb endings barely needs a "yes" word — the verb is the answer. This is a real window into how Latin thinks: agreement lives in the sentence, not in a little particle bolted on.
